title: The Night the Power Went Out
paragraphs: It was late November, and the temperature in Uralsk had dropped to minus eighteen. Kamila Seitkali was sitting in her dormitory room, studying for her linguistics exam. Outside, the wind was howling and snow was hitting the windows like small stones. She was feeling stressed — she had three chapters still to revise and the exam was the next morning.

At exactly 11:47 p.m., the electricity went out. The whole building went dark in an instant. Kamila's laptop screen went black, and the only light was the pale blue glow of her phone. She heard other students in the corridor — some were screaming, some were laughing nervously. Her roommate Zarina was sleeping in the other bed; she woke up immediately and said, in a confused voice: "What's happening?"

While Kamila was trying to find a torch in her bag, Amir was sending messages to the group chat from his room two floors up. "Power is out — anyone have candles?" he typed. Someone in the group replied immediately: "I have birthday candles. Not helpful." Another student wrote: "I was just about to submit my essay when it happened. I want to cry." Rustam replied with three laughing emojis.

Within twenty minutes, the dormitory staff had found emergency lighting and placed small portable lamps in the corridors. Students were emerging from their rooms with blankets, snacks, and phones. The hallway on the third floor became a kind of impromptu meeting place. Zhibek arrived with a thermos of hot tea and a packet of biscuits. "I was practising for volleyball in my room when it happened," she said, still wearing her sports clothes.

For the next two hours, the power stayed off. Without electricity, nobody could study or submit assignments. Instead, students were talking, sharing food, and telling stories. Kamila found herself describing her village in southern Kazakhstan — how the power used to go out regularly in winter, how her grandmother would light candles and tell stories until midnight. "In Uralsk it's a crisis," she laughed. "Back home it was just Tuesday."

The power came back on at 1:58 a.m. There was a cheer from the corridor. Students returned to their rooms. Kamila looked at her open textbook and decided that enough was enough. She closed her laptop, got into bed, and fell asleep within three minutes. In the morning, she discovered that the exam had been postponed — a pipe had burst in the examination building overnight due to the extreme cold. The universe, she reflected, sometimes makes decisions for you.

She told the story to her parents over video call the next evening. Her mother laughed and said: "So the blackout saved you?" Kamila shook her head: "No — it reminded me that sometimes the things you cannot control are the things that bring people together. We were all sitting in that hallway, and for two hours we weren't students with deadlines. We were just people sharing tea in the dark."

That night became a story that the third-floor students told for the rest of the semester. Every time the wind was particularly strong, someone would say: "Remember the night of the blackout?" And everyone would smile, because some memories are made not when everything goes right, but when everything goes wrong at exactly the right time.

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: Kamila, I can't believe you actually fell asleep that night. I was too anxious to sleep.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: I was exhausted! I had been revising for four hours. When the power came back, I just gave up.

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: I was still awake at 3 a.m. finishing my essay. The whole thing was a disaster for me.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: But wasn't it also kind of wonderful? All of us in the hallway like that?

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: I mean... yes, actually. Zhibek's tea was really good. I didn't know she carried a thermos everywhere.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: She does! I discovered that night that Rustam is amazing at telling ghost stories.

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: I know! I was genuinely scared. Which is embarrassing.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: The best part was when the power came back and everyone cheered. Like we'd won something.

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: We had won something. Two hours of not being stressed about deadlines.

vocab.definition: a period when all lights and power fail
vocab.example: The blackout lasted two hours — the whole dormitory was in darkness.

vocab.definition: to make a long, loud crying sound (wind or animal)
vocab.example: The wind was howling outside while the students were studying.
The hallway became an impromptu meeting place for all the students.

vocab.definition: to arrange to do something at a later time than planned
vocab.example: The exam was postponed because a pipe had burst in the building.

vocab.definition: to come out from somewhere you couldn't see
vocab.example: Students were emerging from their rooms with blankets and snacks.

vocab.definition: worried and nervous about something that might happen
vocab.example: Amir was too anxious to sleep — he was worried about his essay deadline.

vocab.definition: a long passage in a building with rooms on either side
vocab.example: Students were sitting in the corridor, sharing tea and telling stories.

vocab.definition: to think deeply and carefully about something
vocab.example: The universe sometimes makes decisions for you, she reflected.

questions.text: "The power went out in an instant." What does "in an instant" mean?
questions.hint: "in an instant" = immediately, extremely fast — in a single moment.

questions.text: The exam was ___ because a pipe burst in the building.
questions.hint: "postponed" = moved to a later time. The exam was postponed, not cancelled.

questions.text: "Students were emerging from their rooms." What does "emerge" mean?
questions.hint: "emerge from" = to come out from a place, becoming visible after being inside or hidden.

questions.text: "Amir was too anxious to sleep." "Anxious" means:
questions.hint: "anxious" = feeling worried or nervous about something that might happen.
